references.text: When Adam and Eve had sinned, their eyes were opened and they knew that they were naked ([ref:1 Mos 3:7|Genesis 3:7]). The expression "their eyes were opened" is used here in a parallel but opposite context: in the Garden of Eden, the opened gaze led to shame, while on the road to Emmaus it leads to recognition of the risen Christ.
God opened Hagar's eyes so that she saw the well ([ref:1 Mos 21:19|Genesis 21:19]). Both texts show that God can open people's eyes so they see what was hidden from them.
The Lord opened Balaam's eyes so that he saw the angel of the Lord ([ref:4 Mos 22:31|Numbers 22:31]). A similar pattern where God supernaturally opens someone's eyes to see the divine.

Elisha prayed that his servant's eyes might be opened, and the Lord opened his eyes so that he saw the mountains full of horses and chariots of fire ([ref:2 Kong 6:17|2 Kings 6:17]). Divine opening of the eyes to see what is invisible.
Elisha prayed that the Arameans' eyes might be opened, and the Lord opened their eyes ([ref:2 Kong 6:20|2 Kings 6:20]). Another example of God controlling people's ability to recognize what they see.

Earlier in the story, the disciples' eyes were kept from recognizing Jesus ([ref:Luk 24:16|Luke 24:16]). Verse 31 is the direct opposite: now their eyes are opened and they recognize him. Together the verses show that God controls the revelation of Jesus' identity.

The disciples told the others that they recognized him when he broke the bread ([ref:Luk 24:35|Luke 24:35]). This is a direct summary of the event in verse 31, linking the recognition to the breaking of bread.

Jesus opened the disciples' minds so they could understand the Scriptures ([ref:Luk 24:45|Luke 24:45]). The same Greek verb (διανοίγω) is used: in verse 31 the eyes are opened, in verse 45 the mind is opened – both times by Jesus' divine action.

Mary Magdalene did not recognize Jesus outside the tomb until he called her by name ([ref:Joh 20:14-16|John 20:14-16]). A similar pattern where the risen Jesus is first unrecognizable, but then reveals his identity.

The disciples did not recognize Jesus when he stood on the shore, until the great catch opened their eyes ([ref:Joh 21:4-7|John 21:4-7]). Another example of the risen Christ first not being recognized, and then being revealed.

Peter testifies that God raised Jesus and let him appear, not to all the people, but to witnesses whom God had chosen beforehand ([ref:Apg 10:40-41|Acts 10:40-41]). Jesus appeared selectively after the resurrection, which aligns with his also disappearing from the sight of the Emmaus disciples.
